Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Troops in Jamaica captured an armed man Monday who had barged onto a Canadian airliner, robbed passengers and held six crew members hostage, Jamaica Information Minister Daryl Vaz said. A hostage-taker commandeered a CanJet flight at Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay, Jamaica. The crew members were not harmed, Vaz said. The hijacking suspect, described as a "mentally challenged" man in his 20s, had demanded that the Boeing 737 be flown to Cuba. The military captured him around 7 a.m. local time. The FBI helped Jamaican authorities handle the situation at the Jamaican government's request, a U.S. government source told CNN. The CanJet flight from Halifax, Canada, had made a scheduled landing at Sangster International Airport in the Jamaican resort city of Montego Bay and was scheduled to continue to Santa Clara, Cuba. Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who was in Jamaica, told reporters that he planned to travel to Montego Bay to meet with Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding. Harper has been following the airplane security breach and may meet with the plane's crew later today. "The hijacking is that from a mentally challenged youngster and not anything that would be of concern in terms of an international incident," Vaz said. The suspect gained access to the plane Sunday night through the terminal in "a breach of security" that "will be investigated," Deputy Police Commissioner Owen Ellington told CNN. The gunman fired a shot in the boarding bridge as he entered, said CanJet Airlines Vice President Kent Woodside. No one was hit. CanJet Flight 918 was carrying 174 passengers and eight crew members, Woodside said. All the passengers were Canadian, he said. The suspect took an undisclosed number of passengers and crew members hostage before releasing all the passengers and two crew members, said Elizabeth Scotton, a spokeswoman for the company that manages the airport. Two of the six crew members who remained inside the plane Monday locked themselves in the cockpit, Vaz said. The suspect's father and Golding, who flew in by helicopter, were among those who negotiated with the gunman before his capture. The country's minister of national security also was at hand. The released passengers were taken to a hotel, and the airport was shut down for a time, Vaz said. The airport reopened shortly after the standoff, Woodside said. A CanJet airliner was on its way to Jamaica, he said, to take passengers on to Cuba or back to Canada. Christian Gosselin, a passenger on the flight, told his father that the gunman demanded cash from the plane's occupants. Vaz confirmed the account. "The guy wanted to have all their money," said Gosselin's father, Alphonse. "He [my son] told his girlfriend to take all the money and just take her passport and credit card and put it in her back pocket." Christian Gosselin was part of a 25-person wedding party headed to Cuba. He and his girlfriend were released by the hostage-taker, and they spoke to his father in New Brunswick, Canada, while waiting for another flight. "I didn't ask them too many questions; I was more concerned for their safety," the father said. "They were a bit shaken up. It was quite an experience." Another passenger, Brenda Grenier, called her husband and said the man apparently got aboard the plane as airport workers were loading bags. Grenier and her daughter were safe, her husband said by phone from his home in Nova Scotia, Canada. CNN's Joyce Joseph, Janet DiGiacomo, Jessica Jordan, Saeed Ahmed and Mike Brooks contributed to this report.

(CNN) -- Jamaican military forces successfully detained an armed individual on Monday following an incident in which he had forced his way onto a Canadian aircraft, stolen belongings from passengers, and kept six flight attendants captive, according to Jamaica's Information Minister Daryl Vaz.

The incident unfolded when a hostage-taker seized control of a CanJet aircraft at Montego Bay's Sangster International Airport. Vaz confirmed that none of the crew members sustained injuries during the ordeal.

Authorities identified the alleged hijacker as a man in his twenties with cognitive disabilities, who had insisted the Boeing 737 be redirected to Cuba. Military personnel apprehended him at approximately 7 a.m. local time. A source within the U.S. government revealed to CNN that the FBI assisted Jamaican officials in resolving the crisis, acting on a request from Jamaica's government.

The aircraft, originating from Halifax, Canada, had touched down as scheduled at the resort city airport before its planned continuation to Santa Clara, Cuba. Prime Minister Stephen Harper of Canada, who happened to be visiting Jamaica at the time, informed journalists of his intention to travel to Montego Bay for talks with Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding. Harper indicated he had been monitoring the security breach closely and might later meet with the plane's crew members.

Minister Vaz downplayed the international significance of the event, stating: "The hijacking is that from a mentally challenged youngster and not anything that would be of concern in terms of an international incident."

Deputy Police Commissioner Owen Ellington told CNN that the suspect had entered the aircraft Sunday evening by passing through the terminal—a clear "breach of security" that would be subject to formal investigation. CanJet Airlines Vice President Kent Woodside reported that the gunman discharged his weapon once while entering via the boarding bridge, though no one was struck by the bullet.

According to Woodside, Flight 918 was transporting 174 passengers alongside eight crew members, with all passengers holding Canadian citizenship. Elizabeth Scotton, spokesperson for the airport's management company, explained that the suspect initially took an unspecified number of people hostage before eventually freeing all passengers plus two additional crew members.

Vaz noted that among the six crew members still trapped aboard the plane Monday, two had barricaded themselves inside the cockpit for safety. The negotiation effort that ultimately led to the suspect's capture involved both the gunman's father and Prime Minister Golding, who arrived via helicopter, alongside the nation's security minister.

Freed passengers were transported to a hotel while operations at the airport were temporarily suspended, Vaz stated. Woodside confirmed the airport resumed normal operations shortly after the situation was resolved, with another CanJet plane dispatched to Jamaica to transport stranded travelers either onward to Cuba or back home to Canada.

Passenger Christian Gosselin relayed to his father that the gunman had demanded money from everyone aboard—an account that Vaz corroborated. "The guy wanted to have all their money," explained Alphonse Gosselin, Christian's father. "He [my son] told his girlfriend to take all the money and just take her passport and credit card and put it in her back pocket."

Christian Gosselin had been traveling as part of a wedding group of 25 people bound for Cuba. Following their release by the hijacker, he and his girlfriend contacted his father in New Brunswick while awaiting alternative travel arrangements. "I didn't ask them too many questions; I was more concerned for their safety," the elder Gosselin remarked. "They were a bit shaken up. It was quite an experience."

Separately, passenger Brenda Grenier phoned her husband to describe how the assailant appeared to have boarded during baggage loading operations by airport staff. Her husband, speaking from their home in Nova Scotia, confirmed that both Grenier and their daughter emerged from the incident unharmed.

*CNN's Joyce Joseph, Janet DiGiacomo, Jessica Jordan, Saeed Ahmed and Mike Brooks contributed to this report.*

*By CNN Staff*

**KINGSTON, Jamaica** — A tense standoff aboard a CanJet charter flight at Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay ended peacefully Wednesday after Jamaican security forces negotiated the surrender of a man who had threatened to blow up the aircraft, authorities said.

The Boeing 737, operated by the Canadian charter airline CanJet, was preparing for departure to Canada when the incident began. Passengers described a chaotic scene as the suspect, reportedly armed with what he claimed was an explosive device, moved through the cabin making demands and holding several crew members and passengers in a state of fear for hours.

**The Standoff**

Jamaican police and military units, including members of the Jamaica Defence Force, surrounded the aircraft shortly after the threat was reported. Sources close to the investigation said the suspect initially demanded to speak with government officials and made a series of shifting demands as negotiators worked to establish contact.

Passengers were evacuated in stages throughout the ordeal, a sign that authorities believed negotiations were progressing even as tensions remained high. Witnesses on the ground described seeing emergency vehicles, armed tactical teams, and airport staff working to keep the situation contained while minimizing risk to those still aboard.

"It was frightening — we didn't know what was happening or how long it would last," one passenger told local reporters after being released from the aircraft. "The crew stayed calm and tried to reassure us, but you could feel how serious it was."

**Negotiations and Resolution**

Jamaican officials said trained negotiators spent several hours communicating with the suspect, working to de-escalate the situation and secure the release of those still on board. Authorities have not released the man's full list of demands, though local reports suggest personal and financial grievances may have played a role in the incident.

By late afternoon, the standoff came to a peaceful conclusion when the suspect exited the aircraft and was taken into custody without further incident. No injuries were reported among passengers, crew, or law enforcement personnel.

"Our priority throughout was the safety of everyone on that aircraft," a Jamaican security official said in a brief statement. "We are relieved this ended without violence."

**Airline and Government Response**

CanJet confirmed the incident in a statement, saying it was cooperating fully with Jamaican authorities and Canadian officials investigating the matter. The airline emphasized that the safety of its passengers and crew remained its top priority and that counseling resources were being made available to those affected.

Jamaican Prime Minister officials praised the coordinated response by police, military, and airport security, calling the resolution a testament to the effectiveness of the country's emergency protocols.

The suspect, whose identity has not been officially released pending charges, is expected to face multiple criminal counts, including hijacking, unlawful confinement, and making threats of violence.

**Ongoing Investigation**

Jamaican police, along with Canadian aviation security officials, are continuing to investigate the incident, including how the suspect boarded the flight and whether he had access to an actual explosive device or merely claimed to. Aviation analysts say the incident is likely to prompt renewed scrutiny of security screening procedures at Sangster International Airport, a major hub for tourists traveling to and from North America.

CNN will continue to update this developing story as more information becomes available.

**KINGSTON, JAMAICA** — A domestic security crisis unfolded today at Norman Manley International Airport after a lone individual attempted to hijack a Boeing 737 passenger jet, holding crew and passengers in a tense standoff that lasted several hours before being resolved peacefully.

According to Jamaican aviation authorities, the aircraft, operating a scheduled flight, was preparing for departure when the suspect—identified by officials only as a Jamaican national in his thirties—breached security protocols and gained access to the aircraft. Reports indicate the individual claimed to be armed and demanded the plane be flown to another destination, though officials later confirmed no firearm was found on his person.

Airport operations were suspended immediately, with all incoming and outgoing flights diverted or delayed. A perimeter was established around the aircraft, and passengers who had not yet boarded were evacuated to secure areas of the terminal.

## Official Statements

Jamaica's Minister of National Security addressed reporters outside the airport, stating:

> "Our primary concern from the outset was the safety of everyone aboard that aircraft. Our security forces, in coordination with airport authorities, worked methodically to de-escalate the situation without any loss of life. I want to commend the professionalism of our negotiators and tactical teams."

A spokesperson for Jamaica Constabulary Force's Counter-Terrorism and Organized Crime Unit added that trained negotiators made contact with the individual within the first hour, engaging him in dialogue that ultimately led to a peaceful surrender.
